title: Case 1: The President of India (Article 52 • Writ Petition)
factualMatrix: Before the Supreme Court of India (Article 32), an aggrieved petitioner challenged an impugned executive notification and enforcement order issued by the Union Ministry / Central Authority under Article 52 (The President of India) of Part V (The Union). Relying on the core guarantee that Establishes the office of the President as the ceremonial Head of State, the first citizen of India, and the symbol of unity and integrity of the nation. and citing Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974), the petitioner sought judicial invalidation for violating constitutional limits and procedural fairness.
framingQuestions: 1. Whether the Writ Petition before the Supreme Court of India (Article 32) is maintainable under Article 52?
2. Does the Union Ministry / Central Authority's executive notification and enforcement order conform to Article 52 (The President of India)?
3. How does Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974) govern the constitutional validity and relief in this matter?
statutoryApplicability: Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974)
modelAnswer:
1. MAINTAINABILITY: The Writ Petition before the Supreme Court of India (Article 32) is maintainable as it raises a direct constitutional question under Article 52 (Part V).

2. SUBSTANTIVE ANALYSIS (Article 52): Establishes the office of the President as the ceremonial Head of State, the first citizen of India, and the symbol of unity and integrity of the nation. Applying the governing principle—'De jure Executive (President) acts on aid and advice of de facto Executive (Council of Ministers headed by PM) under Art 74.'—the impugned executive notification and enforcement order by the Union Ministry / Central Authority must strictly satisfy constitutional bounds.

3. PRECEDENT (Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974)) & RELIEF: Guided by Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974), any overreach inconsistent with Article 52 is liable to be quashed or suitably restrained.

markingRubric.criterion: Precedent reasoning (Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974)) & relief
